title: Abortion After Dobbs
hook: In 2022 the Supreme Court did something rare: it withdrew a constitutional right it had recognized for half a century — and handed the question back to the states.
key_points: For ~50 years, Roe v. Wade (1973) treated abortion as protected under the federal Constitution.
Dobbs v. Jackson (2022) overruled Roe, holding the Constitution confers no such right.
The effect was to return abortion regulation to elected state governments.
The result is a 'patchwork' — access varies sharply from one state to the next.
It illustrates two civics ideas: rights the Court grants it can also remove, and federalism devolving a contested issue.
content_html: For nearly fifty years, the constitutional status of abortion in the United States rested on Roe v. Wade (1973), which treated it as part of a right to privacy implied by the Constitution. In 2022 the Supreme Court did something it rarely does: in Dobbs v. Jackson Women's Health Organization it overruled Roe, concluding that the Constitution confers no right to abortion and that the issue belongs to the people and their elected representatives.
extra_html: NPR's Selena Simmons-Duffin reports that a confusing patchwork of state laws began taking shape within hours of the ruling, and that variation has only hardened since. The civic significance is less about the policy than about the mechanism. First, Dobbs shows that a right recognized by the Court is not necessarily permanent — judicial interpretation can shift, and a protection can be withdrawn. Second, it is a vivid case of federalism in action: with no national constitutional rule, regulation reverts to the states, and a deeply contested question is settled differently in each one. The practical consequence is that where a person lives now largely determines what the law allows. This card describes the legal structure, not the underlying moral debate, and treats U.S. constitutional law specifically.

related.title: Due Process
related.hook: Due process is the promise that the state can't take your liberty or property on a whim — it must follow fair, known rules before it acts against you.

related.title: What a Constitution Is
related.hook: The rulebook above the rules: a constitution sets out how a government is structured and the limits on its power.

related.title: Equality & Minority Rights
related.hook: Majority rule can become majority tyranny. Equality before the law and minority rights are how democracies stop the many from trampling the few.

related.title: How Opinion on Abortion Shifted After Dobbs
related.hook: When the Supreme Court returned abortion to the states in 2022, it didn't settle the debate — public opinion moved, with more Americans taking firm pro-access positions.

prereqs.title: Civil Liberties Basics
prereqs.hook: The freedoms that protect individuals from overreach by the state — like speech, belief, and a fair trial.

flashcards.prompt: What did the Supreme Court's Dobbs decision (2022) change about abortion law?
flashcards.back_html: It overruled Roe v. Wade, holding the Constitution confers no right to abortion — returning regulation of the issue to elected state governments.

flashcards.prompt: What is meant by the 'patchwork' of abortion law after Dobbs?

choices.text: Access and rules vary sharply from one state to the next
A single national statute now governs abortion everywhere
Only federal courts may decide any abortion case

flashcards.explanation_html: With no federal constitutional rule, each state sets its own policy, so legal access differs widely depending on where a person lives.

flashcards.prompt: Which broader civics lesson does Dobbs illustrate?

choices.text: A right the Court recognizes, it can later remove — and a contested issue can be devolved to states
Constitutional rights, once recognized, can never be reversed
Only Congress, never the courts, defines constitutional rights

flashcards.explanation_html: Dobbs shows judicially recognized rights are not permanent, and how federalism can hand a divisive question back to state legislatures.
